title: Title, date and occasion
short: Written after crossing Westminster Bridge at dawn on 31 July 1802, on the way to France; the title's 3 September date is a mistake later corrected.
body: William and Dorothy left London early on 31 July 1802 by the Dover coach to visit Annette Vallon and Caroline, William's daughter, in Calais during the Peace of Amiens. Dorothy's journal describes the city, St Paul's and the river with its little boats as 'a most beautiful sight' from Westminster Bridge, the houses 'not overhung by their cloud of smoke'. The sonnet was published in Poems, in Two Volumes (1807) with the title date 3 September 1802; Dorothy's journal places the crossing on the morning of 31 July, and the Fenwick note says the sonnet was composed on the roof of a coach on the way to France, so the title's September date probably marks when the poem was finished after their return. The opening line is a bold superlative: this city sight outdoes anything the earth can show, an extraordinary claim from the poet of rural nature.

sources.cite: Dorothy Wordsworth, Journals, ed. William Knight (1897), vol. 1, Grasmere Journal

anchor: Dull would he be of soul
title: dull of soul
short: Only an insensitive person could pass this sight by unmoved; 'dull' means spiritually blunt or obtuse.
body: 'Dull' here means slow of perception, lacking feeling (OED sense of mental or spiritual dullness), as in Matthew 13:15, 'their ears are dull of hearing'. The inverted syntax ('Dull would he be') gives the line the weight of a proverb. The sight is 'touching in its majesty', a pairing of tenderness and grandeur that runs through the poem. The poem therefore opens by testing the reader's capacity for feeling, a concern central to Wordsworth's Preface to Lyrical Ballads, which complains of a public whose minds are blunted by city life and sensation.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'dull, adj.'
Bible (KJV), Matthew 13:15

title: like a garment
short: The city wears the morning's beauty like clothing, a simile with a psalm behind it, and a hint that the beauty is temporary.
body: The Psalmist praises God 'Who coverest thyself with light as with a garment' (Psalm 104:2), and the echo lends the city a sacred radiance. A garment is also something put on and taken off, so the beauty belongs to this hour of morning, not to London itself; the smoke and noise of the working day will soon return. Critics note the ambiguity of 'silent, bare' at the line end: 'bare' attaches both to the city (naked under the garment, exposed) and to the following list of buildings.

anchor: Ships, towers, domes, theatres, and temples
title: Ships, towers, domes, theatres, and temples
short: A list of the city's structures, commercial, civic, cultural and religious, laid out in one line.
body: The catalogue (asyndeton until the last item) takes in the whole of London: ships of the Thames trade, towers, the domes (above all St Paul's, which Dorothy mentions), the theatres (Drury Lane and Covent Garden were the patent theatres), and 'temples', a classicising word for churches. The heavy stresses slow the line. The list is neutral, without satire; the commercial city that Wordsworth criticises elsewhere ('Getting and spending') appears here only as form and shape, lit by the sun.

title: Open unto the fields, and to the sky
short: In 1802 London still met open countryside; in the dawn light the city seems to lie open to nature and to heaven.
body: The line joins city and country, a reconciliation unusual in Wordsworth, whose Prelude Book 7 presents London as a chaotic spectacle. 'Unto' has a biblical ring. The buildings 'lie / Open', which suggests both physical visibility and a kind of vulnerability or receptivity. Editors note that in the early nineteenth century fields still lay close to Westminster and Lambeth, so the line is literal as well as visionary.

sources.cite: Stephen Gill, ed., William Wordsworth: The Major Works (Oxford World's Classics), notes to the poem
Wordsworth, The Prelude (1805), Book 7

title: smokeless air
short: At dawn the coal fires were not yet lit, so the usual pall of smoke over London was absent.
body: Coal smoke was a notorious feature of London from the seventeenth century (John Evelyn's Fumifugium of 1661 complained of it). Dorothy's journal observes that the houses were 'not overhung by their cloud of smoke' that morning. The adjective quietly reminds us of what the city normally looks like, so the poem's beauty is a rare and momentary condition. 'Glittering' captures the bright, clear sunlight of a summer dawn.

title: Petrarchan sonnet and turn
short: An Italian (Petrarchan) sonnet: an octave rhyming abbaabba and a sestet rhyming cdcdcd, with the turn at line 9.
body: Wordsworth revived the Miltonic sonnet in 1802, after Dorothy read Milton's sonnets to him on 21 May 1802 (her journal entry; he later said he already knew them by heart), and wrote many on the Petrarchan model. The octave describes the city's appearance; the sestet compares it to nature ('valley, rock, or hill') and turns inward to feeling ('Ne'er saw I, never felt'). The sestet's run of exclamations raises the emotional pitch. Critics note the poem's strong use of negatives ('not any thing', 'Never', 'Ne'er') to express a superlative.

title: steep
short: To soak or bathe thoroughly; the sun drenches the landscape in its first light.
body: 'Steep' as a verb means to soak in liquid (OED). The sun pours its 'first splendour' over valley, rock and hill as though dyeing them. The comparison grants the city the same intensity of light as the natural landscapes Wordsworth knew in the Lake District. The word also faintly echoes 'sleep' later in the sestet, and both suggest immersion in a single, all-embracing condition of light and rest.

title: glideth at his own sweet will
short: The Thames moves freely, undisturbed by the traffic of the working day.
body: The river is personified as masculine ('his'), like Old Father Thames. Usually crowded with boats and shaped by commerce, at this hour it seems to move as it pleases. The archaic verb form 'glideth' gives a slow, gliding rhythm. Some readers note that the Thames at Westminster is tidal, so its flow is in fact governed; the line describes how it seems in the morning stillness, a freedom borrowed from the poet's mood.

sources.cite: Stephen Gill, ed., William Wordsworth: The Major Works (Oxford World's Classics), notes to the poem
Jared Curtis, ed., Poems, in Two Volumes, and Other Poems, 1800-1807 (Cornell Wordsworth, 1983)

title: the very houses seem asleep... that mighty heart
short: The houses sleep and the city's 'mighty heart' lies still: an image of peace that also hints at death.
body: 'Dear God!' is an exclamation of wonder, almost a prayer. The city becomes a single sleeping body whose heart is the centre of London and of the nation's life. 'Lying still' can mean resting or lifeless, and critics have discussed whether the final line carries a shadow of mortality or simply describes deep calm before the day's activity. The poem's peace depends on the absence of people; its stillness is a moment out of time.
